questions.q: What does Git actually store with each commit?
options: A diff (list of line changes) against the previous commit
A full snapshot of every tracked file at that moment
Only the files that are open in your editor
A compressed copy of the entire .git folder's history
questions.explain: Git conceptually stores a full snapshot of the project at each commit, not a chain of diffs — which is why comparing or checking out arbitrary commits is fast and doesn't require replaying patches.

questions.q: Which command moves a changed file from the working directory into the staging area?
options: git commit
git status
git init
git add
questions.explain: git add stages a specific change so it will be included in the next commit; git commit then permanently records whatever is currently staged.

questions.q: Why does Git have a separate staging area instead of committing every changed file automatically?
options: It doesn't — Git commits every changed file automatically
To let you deliberately choose exactly which changes go into a focused, coherent commit
Because staged files are automatically uploaded to GitHub
To save disk space by deleting unstaged files
questions.explain: The staging area lets you build a commit deliberately — staging only the related changes for one coherent commit, even while other unrelated edits sit unstaged in the working directory.

Creates a hidden .git directory, starting version tracking for the folder
Deletes all untracked files
Creates the first commit automatically
questions.explain: git init creates the .git directory and begins tracking the folder as a repository — it does not commit anything on its own.

questions.q: What information does git config --global user.name and user.email set?
options: Your GitHub login password
The branch name you'll use by default
The identity (name and email) that gets recorded on every commit you make
The remote server address for your repository
questions.explain: git config sets your local identity, which Git attaches to every commit you create — it has nothing to do with authentication to a remote server.
